evidence_quotes.quote: Thus, our central research question is as follows: How does the right to secure, adequate access to water become constitutionalised, and how do processes of global norm development play into the social and political construction of the right at the domestic level?

The case selection for this article is based on a most different systems design approach in which we looked for two cases with similar outcomes (constitutionalisation of the right to water in temporal proximity to the adoption of the international norm)
Interviews and written statements from activists engaged in the pro-water right group at international and domestic levels are used to contextualise the information.

We started the search in the 271 documents from the constitution-making process. After excluding the irrelevant documents, we ended up with 84 documents containing references to water and 48 documents referencing sanitation [1].
There is also need for more research on the effects of constitutionalisation of the right to water on citizens’ possibility to enjoy their right.

criterion_notes.c1: No. Although the constitutional norms under study concern the human right to water and sanitation (and background/archival discussions mention water scarcity in Kenya and price/privatisation concerns in Slovenia), the paper empirically examines upstream political mobilisation and norm diffusion in constitution-making rather than household or community water or sanitation service access.
criterion_notes.c2: No under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading; borderline/yes on topic under the plain reading as a legal/constitutional governance study, though constitutionalisation is the dependent variable rather than an exposure governing service access. Under the plain wording of Criterion 2 ('Examines a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor'), the paper examines constitutional legal norms (Art. 43 in Kenya; Art. 70a public-good/non-profit water provision in Slovenia) and political/institutional opportunity structures; however, even under the plain reading of Criterion 2, the full-text decision remains 'exclude' because Criterion 1 and Criterion 4 fail (no service-access outcome is studied). Under the 2026-10-13 clarification, Criterion 2 is not met because the paper analyses upstream international norm diffusion, activist framing, and constitution-making politics rather than how a rule-type mechanism (eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation/tenure, tariff rules, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulation) directly governs household or community service access.
criterion_notes.c3: Yes. Empirical comparative case study (most different systems design) using process tracing, content coding of 271 archival documents from Kenya's constitution-making process (84 referencing water and 48 referencing sanitation), Slovenian parliamentary proceedings, and interviews/written statements with activists.
criterion_notes.c4: No. The outcome studied is the constitutionalisation and textual framing of the right to water and sanitation in national constitutions (de jure norm adoption), not any outcome measuring water or sanitation access, connection, availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion. The authors explicitly note in the conclusion that further research is needed on the effects of constitutionalisation on citizens' ability to enjoy the right.
criterion_notes.c5: Yes for the study's own political-science research question: the comparative case-study/process-tracing design, country cases and archival/interview data sources, explanatory factors (transnational norm diffusion and domestic opportunity structures), and political-legal outcome (constitutional adoption and framing of the right to water) are clearly identified, though no household/community service-access outcome is measured.
criterion_notes.c6: Yes. Full text is written in English.

study_design: Comparative case study (most different systems design) using process tracing, archival document content analysis, parliamentary records, and qualitative interviews/written statements
population_and_sample: Two national constitution-making processes (Kenya, 2002–2010; Slovenia, 2013–2016), examined using 271 archival constitution-making documents from Kenya's Katiba Institute (84 referencing water, 48 referencing sanitation), Slovenian National Assembly (Državni Zbor) proceedings, and activist interviews/written statements
exposure: International norm diffusion / transnational norm entrepreneurs (UN human rights bodies, South African constitutional experts, GTZ/GIZ, EU concession directive) and domestic political and normative opportunity structures
outcome: Constitutionalisation and textual framing of the right to water (and sanitation) in Kenya's 2010 Constitution (Art. 43) and Slovenia's 2016 constitutional amendment (Art. 70a); no household or community water or sanitation service-access outcome is reported
rationale: Excluded (E04: Wrong outcome). Although this is an empirical comparative process-tracing study of the human right to water and sanitation in Kenya and Slovenia, its dependent variable ('outcome of interest') is upstream de jure constitutional adoption and discursive framing of the right to water in national constitutions rather than household or community water or sanitation service access, connection, availability, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion. It also fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2 because it studies norm diffusion and constitution-making mobilisation rather than a rule-type mechanism governing actual service access (and would likewise be excluded under the plain Criterion 2 wording due to the absence of any service-access outcome).
